name: BLINDSIDE announcement trailer - score (one journey)
note: THE SCORE, for TRAILER.md as rewritten 2026-09-10. Change a note by changing a number in
this file. Nothing here is code.
WHAT CHANGED FROM trailer.json, and why. That score was written for six acts, five text
cards and a hard stop at 1:01 under a card. There are no cards and no acts any more: one
continuous journey in seven movements, and the score is now the only thing carrying the
structure. Four consequences run through every number below.
1. IT DOES NOT STOP. There is no `stop` block. The score thins as the machine goes
underground and is about fourteen decibels down under the map, which is a
diminuendo written into the amplitudes rather than a mixer event. The eight
millisecond cut belonged to a text card and the text cards are gone.
2. IT IS NOT MADE OF IRON. That suited a mine. The world is a snowy valley under
mountains coming out of an ice age, so the bed is a slightly stretched harmonic
stack - 1, 2.01, 3.05, 4.12 - which is a struck ice sheet or a thick pane rather
than a bar of steel. STRUCK IRON APPEARS EXACTLY ONCE, at 1:26.6 in `uncovering`,
on the old HAMMER_ANVIL ratios, and it is the first iron in a cave of ice. It is
also the only note in the bed that is hit rather than swelled; everything else in
the piece except the tread has an attack between 0.8 and 6.5 seconds.
3. IT HAS HARMONY RATHER THAN TWO HARMONIC EVENTS. Twenty chords in 108 seconds, all
diatonic, none of them containing a tritone, none of them containing a leading
tone, and the piece ends on the chord it began on. The centre is A and the mode is
aeolian, drifting one flat toward F major through the cave and coming home for the
map. The chord chart is in the section ids:
range      A5 . F . C                       0:00-0:20  wide, no third at first
machine    G . Am                           0:20-0:30  the tread enters
village    F . C . Dm . G                   0:30-0:45  the only melody in the piece
stairs     Am . G . F . Em                  0:45-0:55  a bass walking down by step
cave       Fadd9 . Dm9 . Bb . F/A           0:55-1:25  flat-ward, and the bed lifts
uncovering C, and one struck iron           1:25-1:35
map        A across five octaves            1:35-1:48  where it started
4. NOTHING IS ON A GRID. The old score put nine strikes a second on exact integer
seconds at 60 BPM and its own notes called that the least defensible thing in it.
There is no tempo here. The only pulse is the machine's tread - alternating root
and fifth, plucked, one step about every 1.15 s - and it exists only while the
machine is walking on the surface: it enters at 0:21 with the machine and its last
step is at 0:54.3, at the edge of the hole. Every step is displaced by up to a
hundred milliseconds and up to a third of its own level (`humanize_s`, `touch`),
deterministically, from a hash of the line's id and the strike number - so the same
document always renders the same performance. It is a walking bass rather than a
metronome because it carries the harmony as well as the beat, and its grid is
continuous across the ten sections it walks through: the `at_s` values below are
chosen so a chord change never puts a stumble in the gait.
REGISTER, and this is the best thing in the piece rather than a compromise. tuning.py
reserves 400 Hz - 3 kHz for everything that has to be identified by ear (heard ping 760,
own ping 620->2100, the ratchet 940->2103), and the score is not allowed in it. That
leaves two windows: 20-400 Hz and above 3 kHz. So the piece is a deep bed with a high
frost over it and three empty octaves in between - which is what cold dense air with snow
in it does to sound, and it is also what rescues a laptop, because the frost sits at
3.1-5.6 kHz where a small speaker is at its most efficient and loses nothing. The old
score had to carry a partial at 6.85x to survive a laptop at all. This one does not.
TIMBRE AND PITCH ARE COUPLED, because of the reserved band. A partial is ratio x pitch
and Score.band_report checks every one before the render, so each timbre has a ceiling:
deep <= 92 Hz, body <= 131, reed <= 198, iron <= 116, pizz <= 131, glass anywhere under
400 or over 3000, frost over 3100. Moving a note up an octave usually means moving it to
the next timbre up.
STEREO. The root and the fifth of every chord are panned apart and are never detuned,
because two detuned copies of a fundamental cancel when somebody plays the film in mono
and the bass disappears at the null. Width is bought instead where it is safe: the third
and the upper voices are split into hard-panned pairs a few cents apart, which beat over
several seconds and decorrelate the field, and the frost is always two different pitches
at opposite edges. A split pair at one reflection each costs exactly what the single line
at three reflections cost, so the width was free.

deep.note: The bed. A SLIGHTLY STRETCHED HARMONIC SERIES, which is the whole change of material from the old score. 1, 2.09, 3.42 is a struck steel bar and it belonged to a mine. 1, 2.01, 3.05, 4.12 is what a large plate of ice or a thick pane does: nearly harmonic, so it is a pitch rather than a clang, but stretched enough that its own partials beat slowly against the note next to it. That slow beating is where the shimmer in this piece comes from and it is free. Ceiling 92 Hz: 4.12 x 92 = 379.

body.note: The same material one octave up, one partial shorter so it clears the band. Ceiling 131 Hz: 3.02 x 130.81 = 395.

reed.note: Two partials, so it is hollow rather than bright - a stopped pipe, or a bowed edge. This is the register that sings without entering the reserved band. Ceiling 198 Hz: 2.01 x 196 = 394.

glass.note: A pure sine and nothing else, so it is legal at any pitch under 400 or over 3000. The melody is this, with a few cents of downward glide on every note, which is what a bowed or blown release does and is the only expression available inside one Voice.

frost.note: The high layer, above the reserved band. 3.1-5.6 kHz with an octave over it. This is the piece's top and it is what makes it cold rather than merely low: ice, spindrift, crystals in the air. It is also the practical answer to a small speaker, because everything else here is below 400 Hz where a laptop throws away 20-30 dB and this is not.

iron.note: HAMMER_ANVIL_PARTIALS, from the old score and from the game's own hammer. Used ONCE, in `uncovering`, for the first iron the machine finds. Ceiling 116 Hz: 3.42 x 116 = 397.

pizz.note: The tread. Same stretched stack as the bed, tilted hard so the partials die fast and it reads as a pluck rather than a strike. It is pitched because it is a walking bass: root and fifth of whatever chord is standing.

air.note: One low noise swell, and the only noise in the score. A moving-average width of 192 corners at 110 Hz at 48 kHz. It is here for eight seconds at the head of the piece so the score arrives out of the air rather than switching on, and it is not used again, because the diegetic wind owns that job everywhere else and two beds fight.

sections.note: 0:00-0:08. THE RANGE. An open fifth with no third in it, so the range has scale but no mood yet - a mode would be an opinion about a mountain. Every attack is 4.5 to 6.5 s: the score does not begin, it is found to have been there.

0:08-0:14. The bass steps down a third to F and the third of the chord arrives with it. This is the widening: the same A is still on top and it has become the fifth of something larger. Every swell in this section reaches its peak before the section ends, which is a rule the piece keeps everywhere - an attack longer than about six tenths of its own section smears the chord into the next one.

0:14-0:20. C major, the brightest chord so far, and the floor drops away under it - C1 at 32.7 Hz is the lowest note in the piece and it is here because this is the shot that has to carry absolute scale.

0:20-0:25.5. THE MACHINE. The tread enters at 0:21, on the beat the camera arrives on the animal. Root, fifth, root, fifth, about one step every 1.15 s. Its grid runs unbroken from here to 0:54.3 across ten sections; the at_s values are what keep it unbroken.

lines.note: steps 0 and 2 of the gait: 21.00 and 23.30 before humanising

sections.note: 0:25.5-0:30. Home for the first time. The minor third is stated in the middle of the chord rather than on top, so the mode arrives without announcing itself. Gait steps 4 to 7.

0:30-0:34.5. THE VILLAGE. The only melody in the piece is here, four phrases over four chords, and it is a pure sine because above 200 Hz nothing else clears the reserved band. Each note glides a few cents flat across its length, which is what a bowed or blown release does. Gait steps 8 to 11.
0:34.5-0:38.5. The melody's second phrase reaches E4, which is the top of the whole piece, and comes straight back down. Lit windows. Gait steps 12 to 15.

0:38.5-0:42. The bass comes UP to D2 rather than down to D1, so the voicing closes in - the village is the only place in the piece where anything is near. A quiet D1 keeps the floor under it. Gait steps 16 to 18.
0:42-0:45. The phrase ends on G3 held long, which is where the melody stops for good. Nothing sings again until the cave, and then only in the bed. Gait steps 19 and 20.

0:45-0:47.5. THE STAIRS. Four chords over ten seconds on a bass that walks down by step - A, G, F, E - which is the oldest descending figure there is and is here because the machine is literally going down. The thirds get quieter at every step and the tread thins with them, and the same four notes are stated two octaves up as pure sine - which is how a lament tetrachord is usually voiced anyway, and is also the measured fix for the one passage in the piece a laptop was throwing away. Nothing about this is chromatic and nothing about it is a threat; it is gravity. Gait steps 21 to 23.

sections.note: Gait steps 24 and 25.

sections.note: 0:52.5-0:55. The last built step. Gait steps 28 and 29, and the LAST STEP IN THE FILM is at 0:54.35: nothing walks after this. The tetrachord's own semitone is F to E, at 0:52.5, and the hole answers it: E to F across the boundary at 0:55 is the same semitone going back up. They are the only two semitone moves in the piece and they are the two halves of the same door.

lines.note: the tetrachord again, two octaves up, where a small speaker can find it

sections.note: 0:55-1:03. THE CAVE. The room opens: quality falls to 0.26-0.28, which makes the reflections later, duller and louder against the direct sound, and three of them instead of two. The chord is F with a G in it - an added ninth, the most open and least resolved consonance available, and the sound of a big space that is not threatening. The tread is gone: there is no ground here.

1:03-1:11. Down a third. The lowest bass in the cave and the widest voicing in the piece: D1 at 36.7 Hz against a frost at 5.3 kHz is a gap of seven and a half octaves, with the reserved band sitting empty in the middle of it.

1:11-1:19. The bass LIFTS instead of dropping, and the piece goes one flat further out than it has been. This is the deepest and most beautiful part of the cave and it is also where the bed starts thinning and the frost becomes a real layer rather than a dusting - the world becoming data as the light fails. B flat is diatonic to F major throughout; there is no chromaticism in this piece and no chord in it contains a tritone.

1:19-1:25. F with A underneath it: the same chord the cave started on, now in first inversion, which is the softest way there is to arrive somewhere without stopping. It is also the piece quietly coming back toward A without saying so. The bed is thinner again and sits higher, so the spectrum keeps climbing through the cave.

1:25-1:32. THE FIRST IRON, and the loudest place in the film. C major, the brightest and plainest chord in the piece, in root position with its third clearly voiced - discovery rather than menace. And at 1:26.6, one struck note on HAMMER_ANVIL_PARTIALS: an attack of eight milliseconds against a piece whose every other swell takes between 0.8 and 6.5 seconds to arrive. It is the only thing in 108 seconds that is HIT, and it is the only iron in a world made of ice.
1:32-1:35. Fade to black. The third goes, so C major becomes a bare fifth again, and nothing is struck after 1:32.6. The picture and the harmony empty at the same rate.

1:35-1:48. THE MAP, and it is nearly silent - about fourteen decibels under the cave. One pitch, A, sounded across five octaves: A1, E2 (its fifth), A3, and two A7s a cent and a bit apart so they beat at about 2.4 Hz and shimmer rather than sit. The piece ends on the chord it opened on, at a tenth of the level. That is the same argument the picture is making: this is the place you have just walked, seen from outside, rebuilt out of nothing.

lines.note: the last note in the film
